Surah 21 (al-Anbiya’), Makkan, 112 verses [revealed after Surah Ibrahim]. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

This lam: it is either connected to iqtaraba (drew near), or it is an emphasis on the attribution of the reckoning to them, as in your saying: "Azifa lil-hayy rahiluhum" (the departure of the tribe drew near). The original is: "azifa rahilu al-hayy" (the departure of the tribe drew near), then "azifa lil-hayy al-rahil", then "azifa lil-hayy rahiluhum". Similar to this is what Sibawayh cited in the chapter on "what the stable (predicate) is repeated with for emphasis": "‘alayka Zayd harisun ‘alayka" (upon you is Zayd, eager upon you), and "fika Zayd raghibun fika" (in you is Zayd, desiring you). From this is their saying: "la abaka" (may you not have a father), because the lam emphasizes the meaning of the attribution. This second aspect is stranger than the first. The intended meaning is the drawing near of the Hour. When the Hour draws near, whatever occurs in it of reckoning, reward, punishment and other things has drawn near. Similar to this is "wa-qtaraba al-wa'd al-haqq" (and the true promise has drawn near).

If you say: how is it described as drawing near when more than five hundred years have passed since this statement?

I say: it is near in the sight of God. The evidence for this is His, mighty and majestic, saying: "They ask you to hasten the punishment, but Allah will not fail His promise. Indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count." Also, because everything that is coming—however long the times of its arrival and anticipation—is near; what is far is only that which has already occurred and passed away. Also, because what remains of the world is shorter and less than what has passed of it, as evidenced by the sending of the Seal of the Prophets, whose mission was promised at the end of time. And the Prophet, peace be upon him, said [[It was narrated by al-Bazzar with a good chain, from the hadith of Abu Jubayr ibn al-Dahhak al-Ansari; and al-Hasan ibn Sufyan narrated it, and from his route Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya. On this topic, from al-Mustawrid ibn Shaddad, traced to the Prophet: "I was sent in the very breath of the Hour"—the hadith—narrated by al-Tirmidhi. As for his saying: in the sermons of some earlier figures, "The world has departed, a (ruined) remnant has remained, and only a residue remains like the residue of a vessel," this is ‘Abd Allah ibn Ghazwan. Muslim narrated it from his hadith at length.]]: "I was sent in the nasm of the Hour" [[His saying "I was sent in the nasm of the Hour": in al-Sihah, "nasm al-rih" is the first of the wind when it blows gently before it strengthens. From it the hadith "I was sent in the nasm of the Hour," meaning when its beginnings started and its first signs came. Al-nasim also means the plural of nasma, which is the soul. (‘Ayn)]]. And in the sermon of some earlier figures: The world has departed, a (ruined) remnant has remained, and only a residue remains like the residue of a vessel. When the remainder of a thing, however much it is in itself, is small in relation to its main part, it is fitting to be described as few and short in measure.

It is narrated from Ibn ‘Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the intended meaning of "people" (al-nas) is the polytheists. This is the application of a generic name to a part of its referents, due to the existing evidence, namely what follows of the attributes of the polytheists. They are described with heedlessness together with turning away, meaning: they are heedless of their reckoning and inattentive, not reflecting on their end, nor noticing where the outcome of their affair will lead, even though their intellects require that there must be a recompense for the good-doer and the wrongdoer. When they are roused and awakened from the sleep of heedlessness, and become aware of this through the verses and warnings recited to them, they turn away, plug their ears, and flee.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 21, verse 2–3:

He established their turning away from the one who admonishes and the one who awakens: that God renews the reminder for them time after time, sending down to them a verse after a verse and a surah after a surah, so as to repeat the warning and the admonition in their ears, perhaps they will take heed. Yet listening to the verses and surahs, and what they contain of varied admonitions and insights, which are the truest of truths and the most serious of matters, only increases them in play, diversion and mockery. And the dhikr (the reminder) is the portion of the Qur'an that has been sent down.

Ibn Abi 'Ablah read muhdathin with a raf' (nominative), as an adjective agreeing with the place (of the noun). His words wa-hum yal'abun, lahiyatan qulubuhum are two circumstantial clauses (hal, pl. ahwal) that are either successive or overlapping. Whoever reads lahiyatun with a raf' has only one circumstantial clause, because lahiyatun qulubuhum is a predicate following a predicate, in accordance with His words wa-hum. And al-lahiyah: one who is heedless of something, when he becomes oblivious and inattentive. The meaning is that although they may perceive, the benefit of their perception is so slight that it is as if they had not perceived at all; they remained at the very height of their heedlessness and oblivion, failing to reflect and to discern with their hearts.

If you ask: the najwa, which is a noun from tanaajii (secret conversation), can only be secret, so what is the meaning of His words wa-asarru (and they concealed)? I answer: its meaning is that they went to great lengths to keep it hidden; or they arranged it in such a way that no one would notice their private conference or know that they were conferring in secret. The phrase alladhina zalamu is a substitution for the wāw in wa-asarru, to indicate that they are the ones branded with gross wrongdoing in what they concealed. Or it comes in the dialect of one who says "the fleas have eaten me" (akalūnī al-barāghīth). Or it is in the accusative of place, as a term of censure. Or it is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is wa-asarru al-najwa, placed before it; the meaning being: "These people concealed the secret conversation."

Thus the apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun, to record upon their action that it is wrongdoing: hal hadha illa bashar mithlukum (Is this not but a human being like you?) afata'tun al-sihra wa-antum tubsirun (Will you then approach magic while you see?). All of this discourse is in the accusative place as a substitute for the najwa, that is: "and they concealed this talk." It is also permissible for it to be governed by qalu (they said) with an implied verb: they believed that the Messenger of God ﷺ could only be an angel, and that anyone from among mankind who claimed prophethood and brought a miracle was a sorcerer, and his miracle was sorcery; therefore they said, by way of denial: "Will you approach sorcery while you are seeing and witnessing that it is sorcery?" If you ask: why did they conceal this talk and go to great lengths to hide it? I answer: that resembled a consultation among themselves and a mutual deliberation seeking a way to demolish his affair, and working to dissuade people from him [[His words "and working to dissuade people from him" seem to have a lacuna. In al-Sihah: nasabtu li-fulan nasban: if I opposed him. (ʿAyn)]]. It is the custom of those consulting on an affair not to let their enemies share in their counsel, and to strive as much as possible to keep their secret hidden from them. From this comes the people's saying: "Seek help for your needs through secrecy." And it is traced to the Messenger of God ﷺ [[It is narrated as a mawquf (halting at a companion). He said: "and it is traced to the Prophet ﷺ," reported by al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab (the forty-third and third sections) and Ibn 'Adi, through the narration of Sa'id ibn Salam al-'Attar from Thawr ibn Yazid from Khalid ibn Ma'dan from Mu'adh ibn Jabal. As for Sa'id, al-Bukhari said: he is mentioned with fabrication (wad'), and Husayn ibn 'Alwan followed him from Thawr. He also used to fabricate hadith, as said by Ibn 'Adi and Ibn Hibban. Here, Ibn Hibban said, on the authority of Ahmad and Ibn Ma'in: it is a fabricated hadith. Ibn Abi Hatim said, on the authority of his father: it is munkar, with no known basis. On this topic there is also a report from Abu Hurayrah, recorded by Hamzah al-Sahmi in the History of Jurjan, in which is Shumayl ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Jurjani, narrated by Muhammad ibn Mutarrif and by al-Haytham ibn Ayyub al-Talaqani. From Ibn 'Abbas, recorded by Ibn Hibban in al-Du'afa', in which is Tahir ibn al-Fadl al-Halabi, who is accused of fabrication. It has another route, from the narration of al-Khulafa' for al-Hasan ibn 'Ali, the owner of the merchandise, from Ibrahim ibn 'Ali Ibn Malunah al-Balkhi, from al-Talibi, from Ibrahim ibn Ma'qil with its chain. There is nothing in it other than al-Talibi.]].

It is also possible that they concealed their secret conversation in this way and then said to the Messenger of God ﷺ and the believers: "If what you claim is true, then tell us what we concealed."

[Mahmud said: "If you ask, why did he depart from his saying 'He knows the secret,' when the preceding phrase was ﴿and they conceal their private counsel﴾ ... etc." Ahmad said:

This is one of the cases of following the Qur'an according to personal opinion (ra'y). We seek refuge in God from that, especially an opinion that denies the attributes of perfection from God, the Exalted. What is indicated by ﴿the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ regarding the negation of the two attributes of hearing and knowledge, in interpreting them in that way? Yet in the language, "hearing" (samī') is not understood except as one who hears, and "knowing" (alīm) is not understood except as one who knows. These are derived attributes (mushtaqqat) from verbal nouns (masadir) which must first be understood and established, and then the establishment of that from which they are derived. Whoever denies hearing and knowledge has hastened to deny the All-Hearing and the All-Knowing without realizing it. Our purpose in this work is nothing but to awaken attention to what al-Kashshaf conceals of the perils of innovation (bid'a), so that the reader may avoid them. As for the rational proofs of speculative theology (kalam), they are to be sought from their own discipline. His position regarding such stirrings (nazaghat) that he presents is varied. Sometimes he presents them at a statement that appears, in its outward sense, to suggest his aim; in that case our task is to dispute the apparent meaning, then we may proceed to show that its apparent meaning is the reverse of his intention, or that it is explicit (nass) in a way that does not admit what he claims in any respect. Fairness may also compel us to concede the apparent meaning to him, and then we mention the mode of interpretation indicated by the evidence of reason. At other times he presents fragments of this opinion at a statement that does not admit it and in no way suggests it, his purpose being to make his discourse free of any partisanship and stubborn insistence upon falsehood; we then point out that too. What he mentions at this verse belongs to the category where the text indicates the reverse of his intention, and we have clarified it.]

? I say: The word "speech" (al-qawl) is general, encompassing both the secret and the open. Thus knowledge of it includes knowledge of the secret and more, so it is more emphatic in expressing comprehensive awareness of their private counsel than saying "He knows the secret," just as his saying "He knows the secret" is more emphatic than saying "He knows their secret." Then he explained that by stating that He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing in His essence, so how could anything be hidden from Him?

If you ask: Why was this more emphatic expression omitted in surah al-Furqan in His saying ﴿Say: He has sent it down, who knows the secret in the heavens and the earth﴾? I say: It is not necessary that the most emphatic expression be used in every place; rather, sometimes the emphatic is used and sometimes the more emphatic, just as the good is used in one place and the better in another, to vary the discourse in its variety, and to combine the end and what is below it. Moreover, the style of that verse differs from the style of this one, because here he first mentioned that they concealed their private counsel, so it is as if He intended to say: "My Lord knows what they concealed," so He placed "speech" in the place of that for the sake of emphasis. And there the intention was to describe His essence by saying that He who knows the secret in the heavens and the earth sent it down; so it is like His saying ﴿Knower of the unseen﴾ and ﴿not an atom's weight escapes Him﴾ [cf. ﴿He is the Knower of the unseen; not an atom's weight in the heavens or in the earth escapes Him﴾].

And it has been read as ﴿qāla rabbī﴾ ("My Lord said"), as a report of the words of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to them.

Rather than calling it sorcery, they moved on to saying it is a jumble of confused dreams; then to saying it is a fabrication he invented himself; then to saying it is the speech of a poet. Such is falsehood: it is wavering (lajlaj) (the Sihah says: "The truth is clear (ablaj) and falsehood is lajlaj, meaning it repeats without ever being exhausted." (Ibn Hammad al-Jawhari, glossing)), and the one who upholds falsehood is bewildered, going back and forth, never firm on a single position.

It is also possible that this is a divine depiction of their statements as descending in stages of corruption: their second claim is more corrupt than the first, the third more corrupt than the second, and likewise the fourth is more corrupt than the third.

The validity of the comparison in His words ﴿as the earlier ones were sent﴾ lies in that it means: "as the earlier ones brought signs," because sending messengers entails bringing signs. Do you not see that there is no difference between your saying "Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent" and your saying "Muhammad brought a miracle."

﴿Will they then believe?﴾ In it: they are more obstinate than those who demanded signs from their prophets and pledged that they would believe when the signs came. Then when the signs came to them, they broke their pledge or went back on it, so God destroyed them. So if We had given them what they demanded, they would have been even more prone to breaking their word, and more so.

He commanded them to ask the people of remembrance, and these are the People of the Book, so that they would inform them that the messengers to whom revelation was sent were humans and not angels, as they had believed. He referred them to those people only because they were supporting the polytheists in opposing the Messenger of God (ﷺ). God the Exalted said: ﴿And you will certainly hear much hurtful speech from those who were given the Scripture before you and from those who associate others with God﴾ [Qur'an 3:186]. So they do not corroborate them in what they are engaged in, being a support for the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 21, verse 8:

"They did not eat food" is a description (sifah) of "body" (jasad). The meaning is: We did not make the prophets, peace be upon them, before him bodies that did not eat food. The word "body" is given in the singular to denote the category (li-iradat al-jins), as if He had said: "possessors of a kind of bodies." This is a refutation of their saying, "What is this Messenger that he eats food?" So if you say: Indeed, by what you have mentioned, their denial that the Messenger should be a human who eats and drinks has been refuted. Then what of their saying has He refuted with His words, "nor were they immortal"? I say:

It may be that they meant that he is a human like us, who lives as we live and dies as we die. Or they may have meant: "Why was he not an angel who does not eat and is immortal?" Either because they believed that angels do not die, or because they called their long lives and extended survival "immortality" (khuludan).

"We fulfilled the promise to them" (ﷺ... no, this is the Qur'anic phrase ﴿صَدَقْنَاهُمُ الْوَعْدَ﴾, "We fulfilled the promise to them") is like the phrase ﴿وَاخْتَارَ مُوسَىٰ قَوْمَهُ﴾ ("And Musa chose his people"). The underlying form in "the promise" is "from his people" (ومن قومه). From the same usage comes the Arabic "صدقوهم القتال" ("they were true to them in fighting"), and "صدقني سنّ بكره" ("the tooth of the young camel told me the truth," meaning its age). ﴿وَمَن نَّشَاءُ﴾ ("and whomever We willed") refers to the believers, and to those whose survival holds a benefit.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 21, verse 10:**

"Your reminder" means your honour and your renown, as in ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾. Or it means your admonition. Or it contains the noble character traits by which you sought praise and a good name [[The phrase "by which you sought praise and a good name" is perhaps "and a good name" with only the conjunction "wa" (and). (ʿ)]], such as good neighbourliness, fulfilling covenants, truthfulness in speech, returning trusts, generosity, and what is similar to that,

And how many a town have We shattered, [[It comes from intense anger and proclaims great wrath, because qasm (shattering) is the most dreadful kind of breaking, the breaking that destroys the cohesion of the parts, unlike fasm (splitting).]] By "town" he means its people, which is why he described them as wrongdoers. He said ﴿and We raised up after them another people﴾ because the meaning is: We destroyed a people and brought into being another people.

From Ibn Abbas: it is Hadur, and Suhul, two towns in Yemen, to which garments are attributed. A hadith states: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was shrouded in two Suhuli garments." [[Agreed upon (Bukhari and Muslim) from Aisha, with the wording: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was shrouded in three Suhuli garments."]] It is also narrated: "Hadluri..." [[Recorded by al-Daraqutni in al-Ilal from the hadith of Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, with the wording: "Three garments: two Hadluri garments and a striped garment (hibra)." He said: Muhammad ibn Ishaq al-Saghani alone narrated it, from Ibn al-Hawab, from al-Thawri, from Asim ibn Abdullah, from Salim, from his father, with this wording.

Benefit: Hadur, with an unpointed ha and a dammed jim, is a village in Sanaa near the village of Abd al-Razzaq.]] Allah sent to them a prophet, and they killed him, so Allah set Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar) over them, just as He had set him over the people of Jerusalem, and he utterly destroyed them.

It is also narrated that when the swords seized them and a herald called out from the sky, "O vengeance of the prophets!", they regretted and acknowledged their error, but that was when regret no longer benefited them. The apparent meaning of the verse refers to many towns, and perhaps Ibn Abbas mentioned Hadur as one of the towns intended by this verse.

When they recognized the severity of Our punishment and Our seizing, with the knowledge of direct perception and witnessing, and had no doubt about it, ﴿they fled from their dwellings﴾. Rakd (the word used) means striking an animal with the foot, as in His saying ﴿Strike with your foot﴾. So it is permissible that they mounted their animals, spurring them while fleeing in defeat from their town, when the vanguard of the punishment overtook them.

It is also permissible that their swift running on foot is likened to riders spurring their mounts, and so it was said to them:

﴿Do not flee,﴾ with the verb being omitted. If you ask, who is the speaker? I say it may be some of the angels, or some of the believers, or they may be made successors by being told this even though no one actually spoke. Or the Lord of Might may say it and His angels hear it, so that it benefits them in their religion. Or He inspires them with it, so they speak it to themselves.

﴿Return to what you were made to enjoy and to your luxurious dwellings,﴾ that is, the ease and the comfortable state. Itraf means the excess of blessings, and it is tarfah (luxury).

﴿That perhaps you may be questioned.﴾ This is mockery and rebuke, meaning: return to your bounties and your homes, perhaps you will be questioned tomorrow about what happened to you and what befell your wealth and your homes, so that you may answer the questioner with knowledge and witnessing. Or: return and sit as you were in your assemblies, and arrange yourselves in your ranks, so that your slaves and your retinue and those whose affairs you control, upon whom your commands and prohibitions are executed, will ask you, "What do you command? What do you decree? How shall we come and go?" as is the custom of pampered, served masters.

Or people will ask you in your gatherings for help in calamities, consult you in grave and sudden matters, seek healing through your measures, and be illuminated by your opinions. Or those who come to you and the greedy ones will ask you, seeking rain from the clouds of your palms, and seeking the udders of your kindness and your favors [[His saying "and seeking the udders of your kindness": in al-Sihah, the wind drives the clouds and draws them, that is, it milks them. Also in it: al-khalf, with a kasra, is the adornment of a camel's udder. (A)]] — either because they were generous, spending their wealth to be seen by people and seeking praise, or because they were stingy, and so it was said to them as mockery upon mockery and rebuke upon rebuke.

﴿That﴾ refers to "Woe to us!", because it is a claim, as if it were said: that "claim" kept being their claim. The word da'wa means supplication. Allah says: ﴿And the last of their call is: All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ If you ask, why is it called da'wa? I say: because the one who wails seems to call out for woe, saying "O woe!", and God says: this is your time.

Likewise the meaning here is: We made them combining the likeness of the harvested crop and of extinguished embers.

This is the commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 21, verses 16–17:

Meaning: We did not create this raised canopy and this spread-out bed, nor what lies between them of the various kinds of creatures filled with wondrous and marvellous forms, in the manner that tyrants furnish their ceilings, their carpets and all their adornments, for amusement and play. Rather, it is a dismissal of taking up amusement and play, and a declaration of His transcendence above them, as if He had said: Glory be to Us, that We should take up amusement and play. [Mahmud said: "Its meaning is 'Glory be to Us, that We should take amusement and play...' etc." Ahmad said: Beneath his words "and Our independence from the ugly" lies a buried innovation and error. It is one of the treasures that will be heated in the fire of Jahannam. The Qadariyya (the Determinist-denying school, who hold that human reason can determine what is good) require God, exalted is He, to observe what is beneficial and to do what they imagine to be good by their intellects. They suppose that wisdom requires this. On their view, the Wise One cannot dispense with creating what is good in accordance with wisdom, unlike the ugly, since wisdom requires dispensing with it. It is toward this that al-Zamakhshari alludes, and it is nothing but a tendency that the error of the philosophers (al-Falasifa) anticipated. For this reason they say: "It is not possible for there to be a more perfect world than this one, for if power could produce something more perfect and better and God did not create it, that would be stinginess contrary to generosity, or incapacity contrary to power." Some people from the community of Islam whom we will not name, may God pardon him, followed them in this, if this falls within the scope of pardon. The truth is that God, exalted is He, is independent of all acts, whether good or otherwise, beneficial or harmful. He may refrain from creating what the Qadariyya deem good, and He may do what they deem ugly in the realm of observation. Every existent, whether agent or act, absolutely, exists by His power. Nothing exists except God, His attributes and His acts, and He is independent of the entire world, and of its goodness and its ugliness. "If your first and last, your humans and your jinn, were upon the most pious heart of a man among you, that would not increase His dominion by anything. And if your first and last, your humans and your jinn, were upon the most wicked heart of a man among you, that would not diminish His dominion by anything." O God, grant us the truth and make us act by it.] Rather, it is our custom and the requirement of our wisdom, and our independence from the ugly, that We overcome play with seriousness and crush falsehood with truth. For this He used the metaphor of hurling (qadhf) and crushing (damgh), depicting its nullification, its annihilation and its extinction, making it as if it were a solid body like a rock, hurled upon a soft, hollow body, so that it crushes it. [His words "fa-damaghu" (so it crushes it): in al-Sihah (of al-Jawhari), that is, it struck it until the blow reached the brain. This is the disjunctive "am" that is used in the sense of "bal" (rather) together with the interrogative hamza. It signals a turning away from what precedes it and a denunciation of what follows. The thing denounced is their taking gods from the earth who "raise the dead" [[His words "they raise the dead": al-abshar are the living after death. Reported by al-Sihah. (A)]]. By my life, one of the greatest of outrages is that the dead should raise the dead, some of the lifeless.

If you say: How does he denounce them for taking gods that raise (the dead), when they did not claim this for their gods? And how could they, when they were far from such a claim? For they, while acknowledging God, Mighty and Majestic, as the Creator of the heavens and the earth, as in ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "God,"﴾, and acknowledging that He is capable of all possible things and of the first creation, denied resurrection and said, "Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?" For them it was among the impossibilities beyond the power of the Capable, like a second eternal being. So how could they claim it for an inanimate thing that is not described as capable at all?

I say: The matter is as you have mentioned. But by claiming divinity for them, it is necessary for them to claim for them the raising (of the dead), because no one deserves this title except one who is capable of every possible thing, and raising the dead is among the possible things. In this there is a kind of mockery of them, rebuke, and ridicule, and an indication that what they deemed far-fetched from God is not to be deemed far-fetched, because once divinity is valid, the power to originate and to restore is valid with it. **Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 21, verse 22:**

If you ask: what prevents you from reading it in the nominative (*raf'*) as a substitution (*badal*, apposition)? I answer: because *law* (لو, "if it were") has the same force as *in* (إن, "if") in that the statement that follows it is affirmative (*mujab*), and substitution is only permissible in a non-affirmative statement, like His saying, ﴿and none of you shall look back, except your wife﴾. That is because the most general of the general cannot be affirmed, though it may be negated. The meaning is: "If there were gods other than the One who originated them, governing and managing their affairs, both would have been corrupted." This indicates two things. The first is that their governor must necessarily be one. The second is that this one must be Him alone, by His saying, ﴿except Allah﴾.

If you ask: why are both matters necessary? I answer: because we know that the subjects are corrupted by the management of two kings, owing to the mutual overpowering, mutual repudiation and disagreement that arise between them. It is related of Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, when he killed Amr ibn Sa'id al-Ashdaq: "By God, he was dearer to me than the blood of my own eyes, but two stallions cannot be together among the *shuwl*." This is clear. As for the method of mutual prevention (*tamanu'*, the argument from mutual exclusion), the theologians (*mutakallimun*) have debates and contests over it. And because these acts require that Essence distinguished by those attributes, in order to be established and to stand firm.

This is combined with what is known and established in minds: that all that He does is done by the motives of wisdom (dawa'i al-hikma), and error is not possible for Him. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 21, verse 24:

He repeats "Or have they taken gods besides Him?" in order to express abhorrence at their situation and to magnify their disbelief. That is: you attribute to God, exalted is He, that He has a partner; so produce your proof for that, either by way of reason (ʿaql) or by way of revelation (wahy). For you will not find any book of the earlier peoples except that the oneness of God and His being exalted above rivals is called for in it, and associating others with Him is forbidden and threatened with punishment in it. That is, this revelation which came with the meaning of God's oneness and the negation of partners from Him is what came to me, and it has come to all the prophets. So it is "a reminder" (dhikr), that is, an admonition, "for those who are with me," meaning his community (ummah), "and a reminder for those before me," meaning the nations of the prophets, peace be upon them.

It has also been read as dhikru man maʿiya and dhikru man qablī, with tanwin. Then "man" is the object governed by the verbal noun dhikr, as in the saying "or feeding on a day of hunger an orphan" (Qur'an 90:14–15), and this is the original form; the idafah (construct) is then the idafah of the verbal noun to its object, as in the verse: "The Romans have been defeated in the nearest part of the land, but after their defeat they will overcome" (Qur'an 30:2–3). It has also been read man maʿiya and man qablī, with man in the idafah sense in this reading.

Placing a preposition before "maʿa" is unusual, and the justification for it is that it is a noun used as an adverb of place or time, like qabl, baʿd, ʿinda, ladun, and the like, so "min" enters upon it just as it enters upon its counterparts. It has also been read dhikru maʿiya wa dhikru qablī. It is as if it were said: rather, with them is that which is the root of all evil and corruption, namely ignorance, the lack of knowledge, and the failure to distinguish between truth and falsehood; from this arises this turning away, and from there comes this denial. The meaning is that their turning away, caused by ignorance, is the truth and not falsehood.

It was read as «الم تر» (without the wāw). Also, ﴿رتقا﴾ is read with a fatḥah on the tā', and both forms have the sense of the passive participle (maf'ūl), like al-khalq (the created) and al-naqḍ (the broken), meaning: "they were sewn together" (mar-tūqatayn). If you say: "The rutq (a noun of the verbal noun type, masdar, a noun denoting the action itself) is suitable to be used in place of marttūqatayn, since it is a masdar, so how is it used with ...?"

I say: it is by supposing an omitted modified noun, meaning: "they were a thing that was rutq (sewn together)." The meaning is that the heaven was clinging to the earth, with no space between them. Or the heavens were clinging to one another, and likewise the earths, with no gap between them, so God split them and separated them. It has also been said: "We split them by rain and plants after they had been solid (muṣmatah)." The reason it says ﴿كانتا﴾ (they both were) rather than ﴿كن﴾ (they were) is that what is meant is the group of heavens and the group of earth. Similar is the saying "two black stallions" (laqāḥān sawdāwān), meaning two groups; the implicit pronoun (muḍmar) is treated like the explicit noun (muẓhar) in this way.

If you say: "When did they see them as sewn together, so that this assertion came?" I say: there are two aspects. The first: it comes in the Qur'an, which is itself a miracle, so it stands in the place of something seen and witnessed. The second: the earth and heaven clinging together and being separate are both permissible in reason, so separation rather than clinging needs a specifier, and that is the Eternal, glory be to Him.

﴿وجعلنا﴾ either takes one object or two. If it takes one, the meaning is: "We created every living thing from water," like His saying ﴿And God created every creature from water﴾, or as if We created it from water because of its intense need for it, its love for it, and its low patience without it, like His saying, exalted be He, ﴿Man was created of haste﴾. If it takes two, the meaning is: "We made every living thing by means of water, which it must have." The «من» here is like the «من» in the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: [[It was narrated by al-Bukhārī in al-Adab al-Mufrad, al-Bazzār and al-Ṭabarānī, from the narration of Yaḥyā ibn Muḥammad ibn Qays, from ʿAmr ibn Abī ʿAmr, from Anas. It was also read ﴿حيا﴾ (living), and that is the second object. The adverbial phrase (ẓarf) is superfluous (laghw).

i.e., lest the earth should sway with them and be shaken. Or [it means] lest it sway with them, so the *lā* (not) and the *lām* were omitted. The omission of *lā* is permissible because there is no ambiguity. [[Maḥmūd said: "Its meaning is 'lest it sway with them,' or the *lā* is omitted for safety from ambiguity." Aḥmad said: Better than these two views is that it comes from their saying: "I have prepared this piece of wood lest the wall lean, so I prop it up." Sībawayh said: its meaning is that I prop up the wall when it leans. The mention of the leaning came first out of concern for its importance, and also because it is the cause of the propping, and the propping is the cause of preparing the wood. *Al-fajj* (the wide path): the broad road. If you say: "The *fijāj* (broad paths) carries the meaning of a qualifier, so why was it placed before *subul* (paths) and not after it, as in His saying ﴿that you may follow therein paths, broad (subulan fijājan)﴾?" I say: it was not placed first while being a qualifier, but it was made a *ḥāl* (circumstantial qualifier), like the poet's saying:

*For ʿIzza, a desolate campsite, ancient,*
*Wiped away by every dark, ever-raining cloud.*

[This is by Kuthayyir.] The *ṭalal* is what remains of the traces of a dwelling, and when a qualifier precedes the noun it qualifies, it is a *ḥāl* of it, as here. This is because the view of the Kufans and al-Akhfash is that *ṭalal* is the subject of the adverbial phrase before it, and that it is relied upon. *Mūḥishan* (desolate) is a *ḥāl* of it, placed before it. It is also permissible that it be a subject (mubtada'), and *mūḥishan* is a *ḥāl* of the pronoun concealed in the adverbial phrase. Sībawayh permitted that it is a *ḥāl* of the delayed subject, and its governing element is the omitted *istiqrār* (being fixed). According to him, difference between the governor of the *ḥāl* and the governor of its possessor is not prohibited, contrary to the majority of grammarians. *Al-mūḥish* means one who causes desolation, the opposite of *al-mu'nis* (one who causes companionship). It is also possible that its meaning is "abounding in wild animals." *ʿAfāhu* means "destroyed it." *Al-ismu* (the noun) refers to the description of the clouds, meaning: every black, perpetually raining cloud. It is also transmitted thus:

*Lumayya, desolate is the campsite, that gleams as if it were a lining.*

It is with a kasra [i.e., *khilal*], the plural of *khilla*, which is a striped lining with which the sheaths of swords are covered, and straps that are worn on the backs of bows.

If you say: "What is the difference between the two in meaning?" I say: one of them is the information that He made in it wide paths. The second is that when He created it, He created it with that attribute, so it is an explanation of what was left vague there. It is preserved by His holding it by His power from falling upon the earth and shaking, [[His words "and shaking" perhaps are: "or shaking." (ʿ)]] or by the meteors from the eavesdropping of the devils upon its inhabitants of the angels, ﴿from its signs﴾, i.e., from what God placed in it of proofs and lessons, such as [[His words "such as the sun" perhaps are "like the sun ... etc.," like the wording of al-Nasafī. (ʿ)]] the sun and the moon and the rest of the luminaries, their courses, their rising and their setting, according to a precise reckoning and a marvelous arrangement, indicating perfect wisdom and overwhelming power. What ignorance is greater than the ignorance of one who turns away from them, and whose imagination does not lead him to reflect upon them, to take lessons from them, and to infer the greatness of the One who brought them into existence from non-existence, arranged them and set them in this position, and deposited in them what He deposited, whose essence none knows but Him, may His power be exalted and His knowledge subtle. It was also read *ʿan āyatihā* (in the singular), relying on the singular to indicate the category, i.e., they are alert to what comes to them from the sky of worldly benefits, such as being illumined by its two luminaries, being guided by its stars, and the life of the earth and animals through its rains, yet they are ﴿turning away from it﴾ as a clear sign of the Creator.

Kull (the tanwin in it is a replacement for the genitive noun that is omitted): that is, "They all are in a orbit (falak) swimming (yasbahun)." The pronoun refers to the sun and the moon, and what is meant by them is the class of risings each day and night. They were treated as plural because of the plurality of their risings, and this is the reason for joining the two with the plural "suns" and "moons." Otherwise the sun is one and the moon is one. The pronoun was given the plural-of-rational-beings wa' ending (يسبحون, yasbahūn) because of the description by their action, which is swimming (al-sibaha).

If you say: What is the grammatical position (mahall) of the clause? I say: its position is accusative (naṣb) as a ḥāl (circumstantial qualifier) of the sun and the moon. If you say: How are the sun and moon singled out, excluding night and day, for the ḥāl to be attributed to them? I say: just as you say, "I saw Zayd and Hind unveiled (mutabarrijatan)" and the like, when you bring a description that pertains specifically to some of what the governing verb relates to. An example of this is the Exalted saying in this surah, "And We gave him Isaac and Jacob as an additional gift" (wa-wahabnā lahu Isḥāqa wa-Ya'qūba nāfilah). Or the clause has no position, because it is a new independent sentence (isti'nāf).

If you say: each of the two moons has its own orbit, so how is it said "all of them swim in an orbit"? I say: this is like their saying, "The amir clothed them in a robe and girded them with a sword," meaning each one of them, or he clothed them and girded them with these two kinds, and he suffices with what indicates the class for brevity, and because the purpose is to indicate the class.

They used to assume he would die and so would gloat over his death. Therefore God negated gloating over him by this, meaning: God has decreed that no human shall remain forever in this world, so neither you nor they are anything but subject to death. Since this is the case, if you die, will these remain? And in the same sense is the saying of the poet:

"Say to those who gloat over us: Wake up! The gloaters will meet what we have met.
It was not that cowardice afflicted us, but our appointed deaths and the turn of fortune against us."

Say to those who gloat over us: Wake up! The gloaters will meet what we have met.

It is said of Dhu al-Isba' al-'Adwani; it is also said of Farwa ibn Musayk al-Muradi; and it is said of al-Farazdaq. Al-tibb (with a kasra) means habit and affliction.

The "anna" here is superfluous (za'ida), and it is possible that it serves to emphasize the negation: meaning, our habit or our affliction is not cowardice, but those calamities are our appointed deaths decreed for us, or our affliction is our appointed deaths. Al-dawla means a turn of victory, because it alternates between the two armies. Al-shami' is one who takes delight out of rage at what has befallen his enemy. He likened them to drunkards by way of metaphor (al-makniyya), because they are not alert to the consequences, and his command to them to wake up is an imaginative depiction (takhyil); he explained this with his saying: they will meet from defeat what we have met, and victory will be ours over them, so let them wake from their intoxication.

That is, We test you with what calls for patience among afflictions, and with what calls for gratitude among blessings, and to Us is your return, and We will recompense you according to what is found in you of patience or gratitude. This is called a trial (ibtila') though He knows what the doers' deeds will be before they exist, because it takes the form of a test. And "fitnatan" is a verbal noun emphasizing "nabluwkum" from a word of the same root (min ghayr lafzihi)...

The mention (dhikr) can be good or otherwise. When the context indicates one of the two, it is stated without a qualifier. For example, you say to a man: "I heard so-and-so mentioning you." If the one mentioning you is a friend, it is praise; if he is an enemy, it is blame. [[Mahmud said: "Mention may be good or otherwise. When the context indicates one of them, it is stated without a qualifying indicator. If the one mentioning is a friend, good is understood from it; if he is an enemy, blame is understood from it." Ahmad said: So it is with this. From it is the saying of Musa (peace be upon him):

﴿Do you say of the truth when it has come to you...﴾

meaning: Do you find fault with the truth when it has come to you? Then he began, saying: ﴿Is this magic?﴾ He did not make it an object of the saying or reported speech, because they had restricted the saying to its being magic, saying ﴿Indeed, this is clear magic﴾, and they did not doubt themselves or ask questions. Other than this has already been discussed. They only stated generally in their saying ﴿Is this the one who mentions your gods?﴾ and did not say: "This one who mentions your gods with every evil," because they found it abhorrent to relate what the Prophet says of disparaging their gods, asserting that they do not hear, see, benefit, or harm. They shielded them from relaying their censure in detail, so they indicated it by the aforementioned allusion, just as the believer avoids reporting a word of disbelief and alludes to it with an expression that conveys the intended meaning by indirect reference. Glory be to the One who misguided them until they behaved courteously toward the idols, while behaving discourteously toward the Most Merciful.]] From it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We heard a youth mentioning them﴾ and ﴿Is this the one who mentions your gods?﴾ The meaning is that they are intent upon mentioning their gods with their aspirations and with what must not be attributed to them, namely that they are intercessors and witnesses. It grieves them that any mentioner should mention them otherwise. As for the mention of God and what must be mentioned of Him in terms of His oneness, they disbelieve in it and do not affirm it at all, so they are most deserving of being taken in mockery by you, for you are in the right and they are in the wrong. It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿with the mention of the Most Merciful﴾ is their saying: "We do not know the Most Merciful except Musaylima," and their saying ﴿And what is the Most Merciful? Shall we prostrate to what you command us?﴾. It has also been said that ﴿with the mention of the Most Merciful﴾ means with what was sent down to you of the Qur'an. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: they take you in mockery while they are in a state which is the very root of mockery and derision, which is disbelief in God.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 21, verses 37–38:

They used to ask for the punishment of Allah and His signs that compel knowledge and acknowledgment, and they say: ﴿When is this promise?﴾ So He intended to forbid them from hastiness and to rebuke them. He first mentioned the reproach of man for excessive haste, and that he is inclined to it, and then forbade them and rebuked them, as if He said: It is no wonder that you should be hasty, for you are made to be so; it is your nature and your disposition. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that by "man" he meant Adam, peace be upon him, and that when the spirit reached his chest but had not fully penetrated him, he wanted to stand up. It is also narrated that when the spirit entered his eyes, he looked at the fruits of Paradise, and when it entered his belly, he desired food. It was said that Allah created him at the end of the day on Friday, before sunset, so He hastened in his creation before it set. It is also related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that it refers to al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. The apparent meaning, however, is that the intended reference is the species. It was said that "ʿajal" means clay, in the dialect of Himyar, and their poet said:

*The pine-tree (nabʿ) grows on the hard, solid rock, and the palm grows between the water and the ʿajal.*

He says: *nabʿ* is a tree from which bows are made; it grows on solid rock, not elsewhere, its *manbit* meaning its growth. The palm grows in soft, well-watered land, so it is "between the water and the ʿajal," i.e., the clay. This is the dialect of Himyar, as it has been said. The apparent meaning is that the first half is a simile for the difficult and stingy person, and the second for the easy and generous one. It is also permissible that the first refers to the brave and the second to the coward, due to the hardness of the first and the softness of the second.

And Allah knows best its soundness. If you say: why did He forbid them from hastiness, when He said ﴿Man was created of haste﴾ and ﴿Man has ever been hasty﴾? Is this not imposing what is beyond one's capacity? I say: this is like the desire He placed in him and commanded him to overcome it, because He gave him the power by which he can suppress desire and abandon haste. It is also read: "khuliqa al-insanu" (man was created).

Answer to "law" is omitted. "Hina" is the object of "ya'lam," meaning: if they knew the time about which they ask, saying "When is this promise?", which is a hard, severe time in which the Fire will encompass them from behind and from in front, so that they cannot repel it from themselves or prevent it, and they will find no helper to help them, given that they were in that state of disbelief, mockery, and seeking haste. But their ignorance of it is what made it seem light to them. It is also permissible for "ya'lam" to be left without a transitive object, meaning: if they had knowledge and were not ignorant, they would not have been hasty.

"Hina" is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb, meaning: at the time when they will not keep the Fire away from their faces, they will know that they were upon falsehood, and this great ignorance will be removed from them. That is, they cannot ward it off; rather, it will suddenly seize them and overcome them. Someone who is defeated in an argument is called "mabhut" (stunned, confounded). From this comes ﴿فَبُهِتَ الَّذِي كَفَرَ﴾ ("so the one who disbelieved was confounded"), meaning Abraham, peace be upon him, overcame the disbeliever.

Al-A'mash read "ya'tihim fayabhutuhum" (with the masculine form). The pronoun refers to the promise or to the time. If you ask: to what does the feminine pronoun refer in this reading? I answer: to the Fire, or to the promise, since it has the meaning of the Fire, which is what they were promised; or according to the interpretation of "the promised thing" or "the appointment"; or to the time, since it has the meaning of the Hour; or to the suddenness. It was also said that in the first reading the pronoun refers to the Hour. Al-A'mash read "baghtatan" with a fatha on the ghayn.

The Prophet (ﷺ) was consoled regarding their mockery of him, by being told that he has a model in the prophets (peace be upon them), and that what they do to him will recoil upon them, just as what the mockers of the prophets (peace be upon them) did came back upon them.

﴿مِنَ الرَّحْمَٰنِ﴾: that is, from His punishment and His chastisement. ﴿بَلْ هُمْ عَنْ ذِكْرِهِ مُعْرِضُونَ﴾: rather, they turn away from His remembrance; they do not even bring it to mind, let alone fear His punishment. Then, when they are given protection from Him, they will know who the protector (الكالئ, al-Kāli') is, and they will be fit to be asked about Him.

The meaning is that Allah commanded His Messenger ﷺ to ask them about the protector (الكالئ, al-Kāli'). Then He explained that they are not fit for that, because of their turning away from the remembrance of the One who protects them.

Then he turns away from that with what "am" carries of the meaning of "bal" (rather), and says: ﴿Or do they have gods that can protect them from Us?﴾ (meaning: that can shield them beyond Our protection and preservation). Then he resumes and makes clear that one who is not able to help himself or defend himself, and who is not accompanied by God's help and support, how could he defend and help another?

Then He said: "Rather, what they enjoy of protection and safekeeping comes only from Us, not from any defender who could keep them from Our destruction. We did not give such protection to them or to their fathers who came before them, but only as a provision of enjoyment in the life of this world and a respite, just as We gave enjoyment to other unbelievers and granted them respite until the term grew long for them, and the days of ease and tranquillity extended over them. So they thought that they would never cease to be in that state, neither overcome nor stripped of the garment of their security and enjoyment. But that is empty hope and a false term. ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, diminishing it from its borders?﴾ That is, We reduce the land of unbelief and the abode of war, and cut away its edges by empowering the Muslims over it, granting them victory over its people, and turning it into an abode of Islam. If you say: what is the benefit of His words ﴿We come to the land﴾? I say: it portrays what Allah was causing to happen at the hands of the Muslims, and that their armies and expeditionary forces used to raid the lands of the polytheists and come upon them as victors, diminishing them from their edges.

Recited as "wa-la yasma'u al-summu" and "wa-la tasma'u al-summu," with the verb read in both the yāʾ and the tāʾ, meaning: you (the Prophet) do not make the deaf hear, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) does not make them hear. "Wa-la yasma'u al-summu" is from the causative of "asma'a" (to make hear). Now if you say: the deaf do not hear the call of the one who gives good news, just as they do not hear the call of the one who warns, so how is it said "idhā mā yundharūn" (when they are warned)? I say: the alif-lām in "al-summ" points back to these warners, and it is the definite of prior reference (li-l-ʿahd), not the definite of the genus (li-l-jins). The original would be: "wa-la yasma'ūna idhā mā yundharūn," but the apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun to indicate their deafness and their stopping of their ears when they are warned. That is, they are of this character in their boldness and audacity in feigning deafness to the verses of warning. "Wa-la-in massat-hum" (and if a mere breath of) that with which they are warned touched them, even a little thing, they would have submitted and humbled themselves, and acknowledged that they had wronged themselves when they feigned deafness and turned away.

In the words "massa" (touch) and "nafḥa" (breath) there are three intensifications, because "nafḥ" carries the sense of little and meagreness. It is said: "nafahat-hu al-dābba" (the beast kicked him), meaning a slight blow, which is "rama'a yasīr" [[The commentator's remark "wa-huwa rama'a yasīr" (a slight kick): in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, "rama'a al-faras wa-l-baghl wa-l-ḥimār": when he strikes with his hind leg.]], and "nafaḥa-hu bi-ʿaṭiyya" (he gave him a small gift): he gave him a little portion; and the form indicates the single occurrence (li-binā' al-marra).

The Mawazin are described as "just" (qist), which means equitable, as an intensifier, as if they were themselves justice. Alternatively, the noun is elided, meaning "possessors of justice." The lam in ﴿لِيَوْمِ الْقِيامَةِ﴾ has the same sense as in your saying: "I came to him for five nights passed of the month." Among the same usage is the verse of al-Nabigha:

Ye, I scrutinized its signs and recognized them after six years, and this is the seventh year.

[[Effaced are Qasm of Furtana and al-Fawari', and Juna'ib Uraik, al-Fawari' and al-Talla' al-Dawaqi'.

I scrutinized its signs and recognized them after six years, and this year is the seventh.

Al-Nabigha said it. "Effaced" (`afa) means "remained" and "passed away." Furtana is the name of his beloved. Qasm, al-Fawari', and Uraik are names of places. Al-Tila' are the elevated places. Al-Dawaqi' (with qaf) are the barren places, abounding in dust. "Daqa'a al-rajul daq'an" (like ta'iba) means that a man clung to the daqa'ah, which is land abounding in dust due to extreme poverty. As for the one with fa', it is the place where torrents flow in abundance. "Tawassamtu" with waw means I followed its marks and signs, and recognized them by them. It is also narrated with ra', meaning I followed its traces and remains, and recognized them, that is, those previously mentioned places.]]

His saying "for six years" means that, in the future, six full years will have passed since its time, and this present year in which we are is the seventh.

Had he said "for seven years," it would have indicated that all seven had passed, which is not the intent. So the claim of some that it would have sufficed for him to say "for seven years," but he was unable to complete it and completed it with something meaningless, has no basis except lack of insight.

It is also said: "for the people of the Day of Resurrection," that is, for their sake. If you ask: what is meant by placing the scales? I say: there are two views. The first: the setting up of a precise reckoning and the requital according to deeds, with justice and fairness, without wronging His servants even the weight of an atom. Thus the placing of scales is given as an image, so that the weighable things may be weighed by them. The second: that He places real scales and weighs deeds by them. From al-Hasan: it is a scale with two pans and a tongue. It is narrated that Dawud (peace be upon him) asked his Lord to show him the scale, and when he saw it he fainted; then he recovered and said: "O my God, who can fill its pan with good deeds?" He said: "O Dawud, when I am pleased with My servant, I fill it with a date."

If you ask: how can deeds be weighed when they are accidents? I say: there are two views. The first: the pages of deeds are weighed. The second: in the pan of good deeds are placed white, shining jewels, and in the pan of evil deeds dark, black jewels.

It is read as ﴿مِثْقالَ حَبَّةٍ﴾ with "kana" as the complete verb (kana al-tammah), like His saying ﴿وَإِنْ كانَ ذُو عُسْرَةٍ﴾.

Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid read ﴿أَتَيْنا بِها﴾, which is a form from ata with the sense of recompense and reciprocation, because they brought Him the deeds and He brought them the reward. Humayd read ﴿أَثَبْنا بِها﴾, from the reward (thawab). In the codex of Ubayy: ﴿جِئْنا بِها﴾.

The pronoun referring to "mithqal" is feminine because it is related to "habbah," as in their saying: "some of his fingers went," meaning: "they both came."

Al-Furqan: this is the Tawrah (the Torah). "And We gave it to them as a light and a reminder for those who are conscious of God." The meaning is that it is, in itself, a light and a reminder. Or: "And We gave them both" (Musa and Harun), with what is in it of laws and admonitions, as a light and a reminder.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, that al-Furqan means the victory (al-fath), as in His saying: ﴿on the day of the Furqan﴾ [8:41]. It is related from al-Dahhak that it means the splitting of the sea. It is related from Muhammad ibn Kaʿb that it means the way out of doubtful matters.

Ibn ʿAbbas read ḍiyaʾan without the conjunction (waw), and in that case it is a circumstantial accusative (ḥal) referring back to al-Furqan.

Al-Dhikr: admonition; or the mention of what they need in their religion and their worldly affairs; or honour (al-sharaf).

The position (i'rab) of alladhina ("those who") is in the genitive, as a descriptive qualifier (sifa). Or it is in the accusative, as an expression of praise (madh). Or it is in the nominative, by implication of that same praise.
This is a blessed reminder, which is the Qur'an. Its blessing: the abundance of its benefits and the plentifulness of its good.

Al-rushd (rectitude, being guided to what is good): being guided to the aspects of goodness. God Most High said: ﴿If you perceive in them rectitude, then hand over to them their property﴾. It is also read *rushdahu* (his rectitude). *Al-rushd* and *al-rushd* are like *al-'adam* and *al-'adam*. The meaning of its annexation to him (*rushdahu*) is that it is rectitude like his.

And that he had rectitude of a great standing, ﴿from before﴾, that is, before Musa and Harun, upon them both be peace. The meaning of "his knowing it" (*'ilmuhu bihi*) is that he knew from him wondrous states, marvelous secrets, and qualities that he approved and praised, to the extent that he qualified him for his intimacy and sincere friendship. This is like your saying about the best of people: "I know so-and-so." Your saying this, in its comprehension of excellent attributes, has the same rank.

*Idh* (when) either relates to *ataynā* (We gave), or to *rushdahu* (his rectitude), or to an omitted element, meaning: mention from the times of his rectitude this time.

His saying ﴿What are these statues?﴾ is feigned ignorance and pretended unawareness, intended to belittle their gods and diminish their standing, despite his knowledge of their veneration and reverence for them. He did not give *al-'akifin* (those who cling devotedly) an object, and treated it as intransitive, like your saying: *fa'ilun al-'ukuf laha* (they are devoted to it) or *waqifun laha* (they stand for it). If you ask: why was it not said *'alayha 'akifun* (they cling upon it), as in His saying ﴿they cling to idols of theirs﴾? I say: if he had intended transitivity, he would have used its complement, which is *'ala*.

How ugly is *taqlid* (blind imitation) and the acceptance of speech without proof! How great is the scheming of Satan against the imitators, when he lured them until they imitated their fathers in worshipping images and pressed their foreheads before them, while believing they are upon something, earnestly supporting their doctrine and disputing with the people of truth on behalf of their falsehood. And it suffices the people of imitation as disgrace that idol-worshippers are among them.

﴿Antum﴾ (you) is of the emphasis without which the speech is not correct if it is omitted, because conjoining onto a pronoun (*damir*) that is in the status of part of the verb is impermissible. Similar to it is ﴿Dwell you and your wife in the Garden﴾. He meant that the imitators and the imitated alike are enrolled in a line of error that is not hidden from anyone who has even the least grip of reason, because both groups rely on no proof, but on a followed desire and an obeyed Satan, and because they deemed it unlikely that what they were upon was error.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 21, verses 60–61:

If you ask: what is the status of the two verbs after "samia'na fatan" (we heard a young man), and what is the difference between them? I answer: they are both attributes of "fatan" (a young man). However, the first, "yadhkuruhum" (who mentions them), is necessarily required for the verb "samia" (to hear), because you do not say "I heard Zayd" and then stop, until you mention something of what was heard. As for the second, it is not so.

If you ask: what is "Ibrahim" here? I answer: it has been said that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, or a vocative (munada). The correct view is that it is the subject (fa'il) of "yuqalu" (is said), because what is meant is the name and not the named person. "'ala a'yun al-nas" (in the sight of the people) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning "visibly, observed," i.e., in their presence and view.

If you ask: what is the meaning of the sense of elevation in "'ala" (upon)? I answer: it is used in the manner of a metaphor, meaning that his coming is established in their eyes and firmly fixed in them, like the firm seating of a rider upon his mount and his being settled on it, "la'allahum yashhadun 'alayhi" (so that they may bear witness against him) by what he was heard saying and by what he did, "aw yahduruna 'uqubatana lahu" (or that they may attend his punishment by us).

It is narrated that the report reached Nimrod and the nobles of his people, so they ordered that he be brought.

Your intention in this answer was to affirm it for him while mocking him, not to deny it from yourself and affirm it for the illiterate or the scribbler, because affirming it for him—while the matter is between the two of you, one of whom is incapable—is mockery of him and an affirmation of the capable one.

The act is attributed both to the one who performs it and to the one who motivates it. It is also permissible that this is a report of what leads to permitting their own doctrine, as if he said to them: "Do you deny that their chief did it? For it is the right of one who is worshipped and called a god to be able to do this and more." It is related that he said: "Their chief did this out of anger that these small ones were worshipped alongside him, though he is greater than them." That is, they stood upright when they returned to themselves and brought forth the sound notion, then they were overturned (inkasa) and reverted from that state, so they began to argue with falsehood and obstinacy, and [claimed] that these [idols], despite their being far below the state of the rational speaking animal, are worshipped gods, able to harm them. Uff! It is a sound which, when uttered, shows that the one who utters it is irritated. For this reason they magnified the fire, exerted themselves in publicizing its matter and glorifying its status, and spared no effort in that.

The fire was made to obey God's act and will, like a subordinate commanded to do something who complies with it. The meaning is: "possessing coolness and safety," and this is intensified, as if its very essence were coolness and safety. The intended sense is: "Be cool, so that Abraham is safe from you." This is indicated by His saying: ﴿عَلَى إِبْرَاهِيمَ﴾.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 21, verses 78–80:

"Idh" means: "and mention them." "Idh" is a substitute (badal) for "humā" (both of them). "Al-nafsh" means the wandering of animals at night. The pronoun is in the plural because it refers to both of them and to the litigants who came before them. It is also read as ﴿لِحُكْمِهِمَا﴾ (for their judgment, in dual). The pronoun in ﴿فَفَهَّمْنَاهَا﴾ refers either to the judgment (al-hukūma) or to the ruling (al-fatwā). It is also read as ﴿فَأَفْهَمْنَاهَا﴾.

Dawud ruled that the sheep belonged to the owner of the field. Sulayman, peace be upon him, who was eleven years old at the time, said: "Something other than this would be more gentle on both parties." He insisted that Dawud should judge that way, so he said: "I think the sheep should be handed over to the people of the field, so they benefit from their milk, their young and their wool, and the field should be handed over to the owners of the sheep, who tend it until it returns to the state it was in on the day it was damaged. Then they should return to their respective owners." Dawud said: "The judgment is what I have judged," and he upheld the ruling accordingly.

If you ask: did they both judge by revelation (waḥy) or by independent reasoning (ijtihād)? I answer: both of them judged by revelation, except that the judgment of Dawud was abrogated (nusikha, naskh) by the judgment of Sulayman. It is also said that both of them exercised ijtihād, and the ijtihād of Sulayman, peace be upon him, was closer to the truth.

If you ask: what is the basis of each of the two judgments? I answer: As for the basis of Dawud's judgment, peace be upon him, when the harm was caused by the sheep, the sheep were surrendered as compensation for their offence to the victim, just as Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, said regarding a slave who commits homicide: the master hands him over for that or ransoms him. According to al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, the master sells him for that or ransoms him. It is likely that the value of the sheep equalled the amount of the loss to the field. As for the basis of Sulayman's judgment, peace be upon him, he made the benefit from the sheep correspond to the benefit lost from the field, without the owner's ownership of the sheep ceasing, and he obliged the owner of the sheep to work on the field until the harm and the loss were removed. An example is what the followers of al-Shafi'i said about one who usurps a slave and the slave escapes from his hand: he must pay the value, and the one whose property was usurped benefits from it in return for the benefits of the slave that the usurper caused him to lose. When the slave is found, they return the respective items to their owners.

If you ask: what would the judgment of this case be in our law? I answer: Abu Hanifa and his companions, may Allah be pleased with them, do not hold that there is liability for it, whether by night or by day, unless there is a driver or a leader with the animal. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, imposes liability at night.

In His saying ﴿فَفَهَّمْنَاهَا سُلَيْمَانَ﴾ there is evidence that the correct judgment was with Sulayman, peace be upon him. In His saying ﴿وَكُلًّا آتَيْنَا حُكْمًا وَعِلْمًا﴾ there is evidence that both of them were correct.

﴿يُسَبِّحْنَ﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) meaning "glorifying" (musabbiḥāt). Or it is a new sentence (istiʾnāf), as if someone had asked: "How did He subjugate them?" So it is answered: "They glorify (Him)."

﴿وَالطَّيْرَ﴾ is either conjoined (ʿaṭf) to "the mountains," or it is an object in the accusative of accompaniment (mafʿūl maʿahu). If you ask: why were the mountains mentioned before the birds? I answer: because their subjugation and their glorification are more remarkable, more indicative of power, and more included in the miraculous, since they are inanimate while birds are animate, though non-speaking. It is related that he would pass by the mountains glorifying (Allah), and they would echo him. It is also said that they would travel with him wherever he went. If you ask: how can mountains speak and glorify? I answer: by Allah creating speech in them, as He created it in the tree when He spoke to Musa.[[His saying "as He created it in the tree when He spoke to Musa" is the position of the Mu'tazila, based on their view that the speech of Allah is created and therefore does not subsist in His Essence, may He be exalted. As for Ahl al-Sunna (the People of the Sunna), His speech, may He be exalted, is eternal and subsists in His Essence, and Musa, peace be upon him, heard it when the veil was lifted from him. (ʿ)]] Another answer is that the one who sees them moving by Allah's motion glorifies (Allah), and when they are described as glorifying, it is because they have been made to glorify.

﴿وَكُنَّا فَاعِلِينَ﴾ means: capable of doing this, even if it seems wondrous to you. It is also said: "We used to do such things with the prophets."

Al-lubūs means clothing. A poet said:

"Put on for every situation its garment: either its bliss or its distress."

This is by Labayhas, nicknamed Naʿāma: seven of his brothers were killed, and he would wear a shirt instead of trousers and vice versa. When asked about this, he would recite this verse, until the blood of the seven was avenged. Al-lubūs (with a fatḥa) means clothing. Its division into bliss and distress in the substitution (of the word) is because of the causal relationship. It is also possible that there is an omitted modifier, meaning: the garment of its bliss or the garment of its distress. The middle term "immā" (either) is for enumeration, but the story indicates that the essence of the garment did not change, so it is possible that al-lubūs is a verbal noun (ism maṣdar), though using the pattern fuʿūl with a fatḥa for a verbal noun is rare. It may also be narrated with a ḍamma, in which case it means the verbal noun in its common usage, i.e., "put on for every situation what suits it of wearing."

Either the straight wearing or the reversed wearing. The one commanded to wear it is not present with us. Al-bu's (with hamza) means hardship; its hamza is changed here to a waw to match the rhyme (qāfiya). Between lubūs and bus there is an incomplete paronomasia (jinās nāqiṣ).

What is meant is the coat of mail. Qatada said: "They were plates, and the first to weave and link them was Dawud." So it combined lightness and protection. ﴿لِتُحْصِنَكُمْ﴾ is read with a nūn, a yāʾ and a tāʾ, and with the ṣād lightened or doubled. The nūn refers to Allah, may He be exalted; the tāʾ refers to the craft or to the lubūs according to the interpretation of "the coat of mail"; and the yāʾ refers to Dawud or to the lubūs.

An example is what the followers of al-Shafi'i said about one who usurps a slave and the slave escapes from his hand: he must pay the value, and the one whose property was usurped benefits from it in return for the benefits of the slave that the usurper caused him to lose. When the slave is found, they return the respective items to their owners.

If you ask: what would the judgment of this case be in our law? I answer: Abu Hanifa and his companions, may Allah be pleased with them, do not hold that there is liability for it, whether by night or by day, unless there is a driver or a leader with the animal. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, imposes liability at night.

In His saying ﴿فَفَهَّمْنَاهَا سُلَيْمَانَ﴾ there is evidence that the correct judgment was with Sulayman, peace be upon him. In His saying ﴿وَكُلًّا آتَيْنَا حُكْمًا وَعِلْمًا﴾ there is evidence that both of them were correct.

﴿يُسَبِّحْنَ﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) meaning "glorifying" (musabbiḥāt). Or it is a new sentence (istiʾnāf), as if someone had asked: "How did He subjugate them?" So it is answered: "They glorify (Him)."

﴿وَالطَّيْرَ﴾ is either conjoined (ʿaṭf) to "the mountains," or it is an object in the accusative of accompaniment (mafʿūl maʿahu). If you ask: why were the mountains mentioned before the birds? I answer: because their subjugation and their glorification are more remarkable, more indicative of power, and more included in the miraculous, since they are inanimate while birds are animate, though non-speaking. It is related that he would pass by the mountains glorifying (Allah), and they would echo him. It is also said that they would travel with him wherever he went. If you ask: how can mountains speak and glorify? I answer: by Allah creating speech in them, as He created it in the tree when He spoke to Musa.[[His saying "as He created it in the tree when He spoke to Musa" is the position of the Mu'tazila, based on their view that the speech of Allah is created and therefore does not subsist in His Essence, may He be exalted. As for Ahl al-Sunna (the People of the Sunna), His speech, may He be exalted, is eternal and subsists in His Essence, and Musa, peace be upon him, heard it when the veil was lifted from him. (ʿ)]] Another answer is that the one who sees them moving by Allah's motion glorifies (Allah), and when they are described as glorifying, it is because they have been made to glorify.

﴿وَكُنَّا فَاعِلِينَ﴾ means: capable of doing this, even if it seems wondrous to you. It is also said: "We used to do such things with the prophets."

Al-lubūs means clothing. A poet said:

"Put on for every situation its garment: either its bliss or its distress."

This is by Labayhas, nicknamed Naʿāma: seven of his brothers were killed, and he would wear a shirt instead of trousers and vice versa. When asked about this, he would recite this verse, until the blood of the seven was avenged. Al-lubūs (with a fatḥa) means clothing. Its division into bliss and distress in the substitution (of the word) is because of the causal relationship. It is also possible that there is an omitted modifier, meaning: the garment of its bliss or the garment of its distress. The middle term "immā" (either) is for enumeration, but the story indicates that the essence of the garment did not change, so it is possible that al-lubūs is a verbal noun (ism maṣdar), though using the pattern fuʿūl with a fatḥa for a verbal noun is rare. It may also be narrated with a ḍamma, in which case it means the verbal noun in its common usage, i.e., "put on for every situation what suits it of wearing."

Either the straight wearing or the reversed wearing. The one commanded to wear it is not present with us. Al-bu's (with hamza) means hardship; its hamza is changed here to a waw to match the rhyme (qāfiya). Between lubūs and bus there is an incomplete paronomasia (jinās nāqiṣ).

What is meant is the coat of mail. Qatada said: "They were plates, and the first to weave and link them was Dawud." So it combined lightness and protection. ﴿لِتُحْصِنَكُمْ﴾ is read with a nūn, a yāʾ and a tāʾ, and with the ṣād lightened or doubled. The nūn refers to Allah, may He be exalted; the tāʾ refers to the craft or to the lubūs according to the interpretation of "the coat of mail"; and the yāʾ refers to Dawud or to the lubūs.

Recited as "al-rīḥ" and as "al-riyāḥ," in both places, with the nominative and accusative readings. The nominative is by way of inception (mubtada'), and the accusative is by way of coordination with "the mountains" (ʿaṭf ʿalā al-jibāl). If you say: you have described these winds at one time as violent (ʿāṣif) and at another as gentle (rakhāʾ), so how is the reconciliation between them?

[Mahmud said: "If you say, this wind has been described as gentle and as violent, what is the explanation of that? I say: it is nothing but that it combined both. In itself it was gentle and good, and in the swiftness of its motion it was like the violent one."] Ahmad said: This is like the description of Moses' staff, which is described at one time as a jann and at another time as a thuʿbān. The jann is the slender kind of snake, and the thuʿbān is the large, coarse kind. The explanation is that it combined both attributes: in its lightness and swiftness of movement it was like the jann, and in the magnitude of its form it was like the thuʿbān. So, according to this interpretation, each of the wind and the staff is two miracles. And God, glorified and exalted, knows best.

I say: It was in itself gentle and good, like a breeze. When it passed beneath his throne, it carried him away in a short time, according to what is said: "its morning course is a month's journey and its evening course a month's journey." So its combining the two matters was that it was gentle in itself and violent in its action, along with its obedience to Solomon and its blowing according to what he willed and decreed: one sign after another, one miracle after another. It was also said that it was gentle at one time and violent at another, because it blew according to the judgment of his will. Our knowledge encompasses everything, so we conduct all things according to what our knowledge and wisdom require.

That is: they dive for him into the seas and extract the pearls, and they go beyond that to crafts, professions, the building of cities and palaces, and the invention of wondrous industries, as He said: ﴿They made for him whatever he wished: sanctuaries and statues﴾. God is the guardian over them lest they deviate from His command, or alter or change it, or lest corruption arise among them in general in what they have been made subject to.

That is, he called out to Him, saying: "Indeed, harm has touched me." It is read *innī* with a kasra, either by implying a verb of saying (*idmār al-qawl*, the implicit verb "he said") or because the call (*nidā'*) carries the meaning of speech (*tadmīn*, implying one verb within another). *Al-ḍurr* with a fatḥa means harm in general, in anything at all, and with a ḍamma it means harm to the self, such as illness or emaciation. The two forms are differentiated because the two meanings differ. He was gentle in the request: he described himself in a way that calls for mercy, described his Lord with the utmost mercy, and did not state the thing he sought outright.

It is related that an old woman approached Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Malik and said: "O Commander of the Faithful, rats have walked through my house on sticks!" He said to her: "You were gentle in your request. Surely I will make them leap like leopards, and fill her house with grain." Ayyūb (peace be upon him) was a Roman, a descendant of Isḥāq ibn Yaʿqūb (peace be upon them both). God had made him a prophet and expanded the world for him, and his family and wealth multiplied. He had seven sons and seven daughters, all kinds of livestock, and five hundred plough-teams (*fadān*) followed by five hundred servants, each servant having a wife, children and palm trees. God tested him by taking his children (the house collapsed on them and they perished) and his wealth, and by illness in his body for eighteen years. According to Qatādah it was thirteen years, and according to Muqātil, seven years, seven months and seven hours. One day his wife said to him: "If only you would call upon God!" He said to her: "How long was the period of ease?" She said: "Eighty years." He said: "I am ashamed before God to call upon Him when the period of my trial has not reached the length of my period of ease." When God removed the affliction from him, He restored his children to life, gave him the like of them, and added more to them. It is related that his wife bore him twenty-six sons.

That is: "for Our mercy towards the worshippers" (*li-raḥmatinā al-ʿābidīn*), and We remember them with goodness and do not forget them; or it is a mercy from Us to Ayyūb and a reminder to others among the worshippers, so that they may be patient as he was patient, and be rewarded as he was rewarded in this world and the next.
