It was said that Dhu'l-Kifl is Ilyas. It was also said that he is Zakariyya, and that he is Yusha' ibn Nun. It seems he was named thus because he was truly one who had a share of fortune from God and was blessed with good fortune (al-majdud).[[His statement "al-majdud" in al-Sihah: "al-jadd" means fortune and luck. You say: "Jadadta, ya fulan," meaning you became one with good fortune, so you are jadid (fortunate) and hazhzhiz (lucky), and majdud (blessed by fortune) and mahzuz (favoured). (ʿ)]] It was also said that he had double the deeds of the prophets of his time and double their reward. It was also said that five of the prophets had two names each: Israel and Ya'qub; Ilyas and Dhu'l-Kifl; 'Isa and al-Masih; Yunus and Dhu'n-Nun; Muhammad and Ahmad. May the blessings and peace of God be upon them all.

The fish (al-nun), so it is attributed to it.

*Barama bi-qawmihi* ("he grew weary of his people"): [[his saying "barama bi-qawmihi" means he became fed up with them and disgusted by them, as stated in al-Sihah (the lexicon by al-Jawhari). (Ed.)]] because of how long he had admonished them without their taking heed, and they persisted in their disbelief. So he broke with them and thought that this was permissible, since he did it only out of zeal for God, a sense of honour for His religion, and hatred of disbelief and its people. He should have been patient and waited for God's permission to emigrate from them, but he was tried by being in the belly of the fish.

The meaning of his being angry with his people (*mughadabatihi li-qawmihi*) is that he angered them by leaving, because they feared that punishment would befall them as a result. Abu Sharaf read *mughdaban* (with the verb in the form that makes it transitive, meaning "making [them] angry"). It has been read *naqdura* and *naqaddara*, both lightened and heavy, and *yaqdura* with the *ya'* and lightened, and *yuqaddara*, passive, lightened and heavy. It has been explained as "he was constricted" and as "God's decree against him as a punishment."

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he entered upon Muʿawiya and said: "The waves of the Qur'an struck me last night, and I drowned in them, and I found no deliverance for myself except through you." He said: "And what is it, O Muʿawiya?" Then he recited this verse, and said: "Does the Prophet of God think that We will not decree (*naqdira*) against him?" He said: "This is from *qadar* (divine decree), not from *qudra* (power)." The lightened form may be explained as *qudra* (power), in the sense that We did not exercise Our power over him. It may also be a figure of speech, meaning: his condition was portrayed as that of one who thought that We would not decree against him in his opposition to his people, without waiting for God's command. It is also possible that this thought came to him through the whispering of Satan, and then he repelled it and turned it back with proof, as the true believer does with the prods of Satan and what he whispers to him at all times. From this is God's saying ﴿and you think about God with various thoughts﴾, and the address is to the believers.

*Fi al-zulumat* ("in the darkness"): in the intense, dense darkness within the belly of the fish, like His saying ﴿God took away their light and left them in darkness﴾ and His saying ﴿they bring them out from the light into the darknesses﴾. It was said: the darkness of the belly of the fish, the sea, and the night. It was also said: a larger fish swallowed his fish, so he was in the darkness of the bellies of two fish and the darkness of the sea.

*Anna la ilaha illa anta* ("that there is no god but You"): meaning, "that there is no god but You," or it is in the sense of "i.e." (*ay*).

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "No one in distress calls upon God with this supplication except that it is answered for him." [[Related by al-Tirmidhi, al-Hakim, and al-Bayhaqi in Shuʿab al-Iman, among the seventy, from the narration of Ibrahim ibn Muhammad ibn Saʿd, from his father, from his grandfather Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The supplication of Dhu al-Nun when he called out while in the belly of the fish: 'There is no god but You, glory be to You, indeed I have been of the wrongdoers.' No Muslim man has ever called upon God with it for anything except that God answered him." Al-Tirmidhi said: some of them related it from Ibrahim, from his grandfather, and did not say "from his father." End. It has supporting narrations: al-Hakim related it through Kathir ibn Zayd, from al-Muttalib ibn Hantab, from Musʿab ibn Saʿd, from his father, with the wording: "Shall I not inform you of something which, when distress or affliction befalls one of you, if he calls upon God with it, will be relieved for him?" They said: "Yes, O Messenger of God." He said: "The supplication of Dhu al-Nun: there is no god but You, glory be to You, indeed I have been of the wrongdoers." Al-Hakim also related it through Maʿmar ibn Sulayman, from Maʿmar, from al-Zuhri, from Abu Umama ibn Sahl ibn Hunayf, from Saʿd.]]

And from al-Hasan: "By God, he was not saved except by his acknowledgment against himself of wrongdoing."

nunjī and nunajjī. And najjā (نجى). The nūn (ن) is not assimilated (idgham, merging a letter into the following one) into the jīm (ج). As for whoever strains to make it sound correct by treating it as a verb and saying "najā al-najā' al-mu'minīn" (نجى النجاء المؤمنين), dropping the yā' (ي) and attributing the verb to its verbal noun (maṣdar), and putting al-mu'minīn (المؤمنين) in the accusative governed by al-najā' (النجاء), he is a far-fetched and frigid strainer.

Zakariyya asked his Lord to grant him a child who would inherit from him and not leave him alone without an heir. Then he referred his affair to Allah in submission, saying: ﴿And You are the best of inheritors.﴾ That is: if You do not grant me one who will inherit from me, I will not mind, for You are the best of inheritors.

Making his wife fit for childbearing after she had been barren. It was also said: improving her character, for she had a bad temper.

The pronoun refers to the prophets mentioned (peace be upon them). He means that they deserved to have their requests answered only because they hastened to the doors of good and competed in attaining them, as those who desire things and are earnest about them do. It is also read ﴿raghaban wa rahaban﴾ with the sukun (on the ba'), and this is like His saying, ﴿He fears the Hereafter and hopes for the mercy of his Lord﴾. ﴿Humbly submissive (khashi'in)﴾: al-Hasan said: humbled before the command of Allah. It is narrated from Mujahid: khushu' is the constant fear in the heart. It was also said: humble.

Al-A'mash was asked about this and said: As for me, I asked Ibrahim, and he said: "Do you not know?" I said: "Inform me." He said: "It is between him and Allah when he lets down his curtain and closes his door, so that Allah sees good in him. Perhaps you think that he eats coarse food, wears coarse clothing, and lowers his head."

She guarded her chastity completely, against both the lawful and the unlawful, as she herself said: ﴿No man has touched me, nor have I been unchaste﴾. If you say: "Breathing the spirit into the body is an expression for giving it life. God Most High said: ﴿So when I have fashioned him and breathed into him of My spirit﴾, meaning, I gave him life. And if that is established, then His words ﴿So We breathed into her of Our spirit﴾ are obviously problematic, because they would indicate the giving of life to Mary." I say: its meaning is, We breathed the spirit into Jesus within her, that is, We gave him life in her womb. [[Mahmud said: "If you say, breathing the spirit into the body is an expression for giving it life, and then its meaning would be, We gave life to Mary, and that would be problematic. I say: its meaning is, We breathed the spirit into Jesus in Mary, that is, We gave him life in her womb, end of his words." Ahmad said: Al-Zamakhshari, in His Mighty and Majestic words ﴿When We inspired to your mother what is inspired, saying: Cast him into the chest, then cast it into the river, and let the river throw it onto the bank﴾, chose that all the pronouns refer back to Musa. As for the first, there is no problem with it. As for the chest, when it is cast into the river with Musa in it, then Musa has been cast into the river. And likewise the third. Others chose that the last two pronouns refer back to the chest, because it was understood from His words ﴿then cast it into the river﴾ that the intended referent is the chest, and Musa was not cast into the river. Al-Zamakhshari treated the casting of the chest into the river with Musa in it as equivalent to casting him into the river. And in this verse there is a confirmation of what he chose, for God Most High treated the breathing of the spirit into Jesus, because he was in Mary's womb, as equivalent to breathing the spirit into Mary, so He expressed it with what the apparent sense conveys.]] And similar to this is when a piper says: "I blew into the house of so-and-so," meaning, I blew into the pipe in his house. It is also permissible that the meaning be: We performed the breathing into Mary from Our spirit, which is Gabriel, peace be upon him, because he breathed into the opening of her garment, so the breath reached her womb. If you say: "Why was it not said 'two signs,' as He said ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs﴾?" I say: because their condition together is one sign, namely her giving birth to him without a father.

Al-Umma: the religion (al-milla). This is a reference to the religion of Islam, meaning: the religion of Islam is your religion, which you must adhere to and not deviate from. It is referred to as one religion, not divided, "and I am your Lord, so worship Me" (﴿وَأَنَا رَبُّكُمْ فَاعْبُدُونِ﴾).

Al-Hasan read ummatukum in the accusative (naṣb) as a substitute (badal) for this (hadhihi), and read ummatun in the nominative (raf') as the predicate (khabar). He also reportedly read both in the nominative, as two predicates for this (hadhihi). Or he intended a new subject (mubtada') for the second, and the address is to people in general (li-l-nās kāffa).

Originally it would be: "and you (plural) cut apart." However, the speech shifted to the third person (ghaybah) in the manner of iltifat, as if He were reproaching them to others for what they had corrupted and denouncing their act in their eyes, saying to them: "Do you not see the enormity of what these people committed in the religion of Allah?" The meaning is: they made the matter of their religion into pieces among themselves (qit'an), just as a group divides a thing and shares it out, so that one gets a portion of it and another gets a portion, as a figure of their disagreement about it and their becoming sects (firaq) and diverse parties (ahzab). Then He threatened them that these divided groups will return to Him, so He is the one who will call them to account and recompense them.

Kufran (ingratitude, denial): a metaphor for the deprivation of reward, just as shukr (gratitude) is a metaphor for granting it when God is called Shakur (the Most Appreciative).

He has negated it using the negation of the genus (nafy al-jins), so that it is more emphatic than saying: "So We shall not deny his effort" (فلا نكفر سعيه) and "Indeed, We record it for him" (وَإِنَّا لَهُ كاتِبُونَ), meaning: We are the ones who record that effort and inscribe it in the ledger of his deeds. Whatever We inscribe is not lost, and its doer is rewarded for it.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 21, verses 95–96:

The word harām (forbidden) is borrowed for something whose existence is impossible. From this is the saying of the Mighty and Majestic, ﴿Indeed, Allah has forbidden them to the disbelievers﴾, meaning: He prevented them from them, and refused that they should belong to them. It is also read: ḥarama and ḥaram, with fatḥa and kasra, and ḥarrama and ḥarrama.

The meaning of ﴿We have destroyed it﴾ is: We resolved to destroy it, or We decreed its destruction. The meaning of "return" is: returning from disbelief to Islam and turning penitently (to Allah). The sense of the verse is: a people whom Allah has resolved to destroy cannot be imagined to return and repent, until the Resurrection comes; then they will return and say, ﴿O woe to us! Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 21, verse 98–100:

What is narrated supports this: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered the mosque while the chieftains of Quraysh were in al-Hatim, and around the Ka'bah were three hundred and sixty idols. He sat with them, and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith came up to him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spoke with him until he silenced him. Then he recited to them, "Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah..." (the verse). Then 'Abd Allah ibn al-Za'bara came by and saw them whispering, and said: "What is this discussion of yours?" Al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah informed him of the words of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). 'Abd Allah said: "By Allah, if I had found him, I would have debated him, so call him." Ibn al-Za'bara said: "Did you say that?" He said: "Yes." He said: "I have defeated you, by the Lord of the Ka'bah. Did not the Jews worship 'Uzayr, and the Christians worship the Messiah, and the Banu Mulayh worship the angels?"

He (ﷺ) said: "Rather, they worshipped the devils who commanded them to that." [[This was related by al-Tha'labi and then al-Baghawi without an isnad. I have not found it in this form except as a composite. As for its beginning, it is in al-Tabarani's al-Saghir at its end, from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered Makkah on the day of the Conquest, and on the Ka'bah were three hundred and sixty idols whose feet were fastened with lead" – the hadith. (the verse) was revealed, it grieved Quraysh and they said: 'He insults our gods.' If you say: Why were they joined with their gods? I say: because they will continue, through their being joined with them, in increased grief and sorrow, since what befell them was on account of them. And looking upon the face of the enemy is a kind of punishment. Also, because they had supposed that they would seek their intercession in the Hereafter and benefit from their intercession; so when they encounter the matter contrary to what they had estimated, nothing will be more hateful to them than them.

If you say: If by "what you worship" you mean the idols, what is the meaning of "for them therein is a groaning (zafir)"? I say: when they and their idols are in one *qarn* [[His saying "qarn" is a rope by which two camels are tied together, according to al-Sihah. It is also read with a sukun on the *sad*, as a verbal noun described as such. It is read *haṭab* and *haḍab* with a *dad*, vowelled and unvowelled.

And from Ibn Mas'ud: they will be placed in coffins of fire, so they will not hear. And it is permissible that Allah makes them deaf just as He makes them blind.

The element governing "the day We fold" is "they will not be grieved" (لا يحزنهم). Alternatively, it is "the terror" (الفزع), or "the angels will meet them" (تتلقاهم). It has also been read as "the heaven will be folded" (تطوى السماء), with the verb in the passive. As-Sijjil is of the form al-'Utull [[His saying "of the form al-'utull": al-'utull means the coarse, harsh one. God Most High says, ﴿coarse, moreover, and of doubtful birth﴾ (68:13). Al-'utull also means a thick spear. A man described as 'atil, with a kasra, is extremely coarse, according to al-Sihah. (ع)]]. It is also pronounced as-sijill, in the pattern of a bucket. A reading with a kasra is also reported, meaning the sheet or scroll. That is, just as the parchment (الطومار) is folded for writing, that is, so that something may be written on it, or so that it may be the thing written on. This is because "kitab" is originally a verbal noun, like "bina'", and then it is applied to the thing written. Whoever reads it as a plural means "for the written things," that is, for the many meanings written in it.

It is said that as-Sijjil is an angel who folds the records of the children of Adam when they are raised up to him. It is also said that he was a scribe of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). On this view, "al-kitab" is the name of the sheet on which things are written.

"Awwala khalq" is the object of "nu'idu," which is explained by the following "nu'iduhu." The kaf is "kaffa" (restrained) by "ma." The meaning is: We will restore the first creation as We began it. The restoration is compared with the beginning, because both are equally within God's power. If you ask: what is the "first creation" that He would restore as He began it? I answer: its first act is bringing it into existence from non-existence. Just as He brought it into existence first from non-existence, He will bring it back a second time from non-existence.

[[Mahmud said: "If you ask what the first creation is, such that He restores it as He began it? I answer: the first creation is its bringing into being from non-existence. Just as He brought it into being first from non-existence, He brings it back a second time from non-existence." I say: he has here, concerning the resurrection, returned to the truth and retracted what he said in the surah of Maryam, where he explained the restoration as the gathering together of what is scattered only. However, he spoiled the purity of his acknowledgment of the truth by explaining His words ﴿We were doing﴾ (إِنَّا كُنَّا فاعِلِينَ) as the power to act. It does not follow from this that the power to act necessarily results in the act, taking into account that what is promised is not the restoration of bodies from non-existence, even though power is capable of that. Rather, it is the restoration of parts to their forms, gathered and joined together, as he stated earlier in the surah of Maryam. Unless what led him to explain the verb as power was that God mentions it in the past tense while the restoration is in the future, so he was compelled to read the verb as power, and he came close to the truth. Nevertheless, the truth is that the verb remains on its apparent meaning, because future acts whose occurrence God knows are, in reality, like past ones. For this reason the future is expressed by the past in many places in the Mighty Book.

The purpose is to announce the certainty of its occurrence, and God knows best.]]. If you ask: why is "khalq" indefinite? I answer: it is like your saying, "he is the first man who came to me," meaning the first of the men, but you made it singular and indefinite in order to detail them man by man. Likewise the meaning of "awwala khalq" is "the first of creation," in the sense of "the first of the creatures," because "khalq" is a verbal noun that is not pluralized.

There is another possibility: the kaf is in the accusative governed by a hidden verb, which is explained by "nu'iduhu," and "ma" is a relative pronoun. That is: We will restore the like of that which We began; We will restore it. "Awwala khalq" is an adverbial complement of "bada'na," meaning: the first thing that was created. Or it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of the relative that has been dropped from the wording but remains in the meaning.

"Wa'dan" is an emphatic verbal noun, since His saying "nu'iduhu" is a promise of the restoration. "Inna kunna fa'ilin" means: We are able to do that.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 21, verse 105:

From al-Sha'bi (may Allah have mercy on him): the Zabur of Dawud (peace be upon him), and the Dhikr is the Tawrat (Torah). It has also been said that "al-Dhikr" is a generic name for what was revealed to the prophets of books. And "al-Dhikr" is Umm al-Kitab (the Mother of the Book), meaning the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh). The meaning is: the believers will inherit the earth after the disbelievers are driven out, as in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And We caused the people who had been deemed weak to inherit the eastern and western parts of the land﴾ [7:137], and ﴿Musa said to his people: "Seek help in Allah and be patient. Indeed, the earth belongs to Allah; He gives it as an inheritance to whomever He wills of His servants, and the good outcome is for the righteous."﴾ [7:128]

From Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him): it is the land of Paradise. It has also been said: it is the Holy Land, which the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) will inherit.

The reference is to what is mentioned in this surah: the reports, the promise, the threat, and the admonitions that reach the heart. As for *al-balagh* (the conveying or sufficiency), it means adequacy, and that by which the desired aim is attained.

He was sent as a mercy to the worlds (ﷺ), because he brought that which makes them happy if they follow him. As for one who opposes and does not follow, he has brought (the loss) upon himself, since he has forfeited his share of it. Its example is this: God causes a copious spring to gush forth, so that some people water their crops and livestock with its water and prosper, while other people who neglect irrigation are left with nothing. The gushing spring is in itself a blessing from God and a mercy to both groups, but the lazy one has made it a trial for himself, since he has deprived himself of what would have benefited him. It has also been said: his being a mercy to the wicked lies in the fact that their punishment was delayed on account of him, and they were made secure from the punishment of total annihilation.

Indeed, "innama" is used either to restrict a judgment to a thing, or to restrict a thing to a judgment, as in your saying: "Innama Zayd qa'im" (Zayd is only standing), and "Innama yaqum Zayd" (only Zayd stands). Both examples are combined in this verse, because "innama yuha ilayya" (it is only revealed to me) with its subject is in the position of "innama yaqum Zayd," and "annama ilahukum ilahun wahid" (your God is only one God) is in the position of "innama Zayd qa'im." The benefit of their combination is to indicate that the revelation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is restricted to Allah's exclusive claim to oneness. In His words, "Fa-hal antum muslimun" (So will you submit?), there is the indication that revelation coming in this manner obliges you to make your monotheism pure for Allah and to renounce rivals (andad). And in it there is the indication that the attribute of oneness may validly have hearing (sam') as its means of knowledge. And it is permissible that the meaning be:

that "alladhi yuha ilayya" (what is revealed to me), so that "ma" is a relative pronoun (mawsula).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 21, verses 109–111:

Ādhana (āmadhana): transferred from adhina, meaning "to know," but its use became common in the sense of giving warning. From it is the saying of God Most High, ﴿then be informed of war from Allah and His Messenger﴾, and the verse of Ibn Hilliza:

āthanatnā bi-baynihā Asmā' ... rubba thāwin yamillu minhu al-thawā'
("Asma' informed us of her parting, and many a sojourner grows weary of his lingering.")

This is the opening line of al-Harith ibn Hilliza's Mu'allaqa. Adhina al-shay' means he knew it by the sense of hearing (the ear), and it was extended until it came to mean knowledge in general. Ādhanahu (with the long vowel) means he informed him. Al-bayn is a verbal noun meaning distance and separation. It has been mentioned that "Asma'" derives from wasāma, meaning beauty. Al-thāwī means the one who resides.

Al-malal is weariness, and al-thawā' is residence. He says: she informed us of her separation. And many a sick person grows weary of people's company in his stay, though she is not like that. This is omitted because the meaning is known from the context.

The meaning is: "I, after your turning away and your aversion from accepting what has been presented to you concerning the obligation of affirming God's oneness and exalting Him above rivals and partners, am like a man who has a truce with his enemies, then senses treachery from them, so he throws back the covenant to them, makes the repudiation public and spreads it, and informs all of them of it ﴿on equal terms﴾, meaning equal in being informed of it; he did not conceal it from any of them, and he disclosed it to all of them, and he stripped the staff of its bark." [Note: the word "lihā'ihā" in al-Sihah: al-lihā' (with a long vowel) is the bark of a tree.] ﴿And what you are promised﴾ of the victory of the Muslims over you is certain to come, and humiliation and abasement will inevitably befall you, though I do not know when that will be, because God has not taught me His knowledge nor informed me of it. God is knowing; nothing He is aware of is hidden from Him, whether what you openly say of the words of those who slander Islam, or what you conceal in your hearts of rancor and enmity toward the Muslims, and He will repay you for it.

And I do not know; perhaps the delay of this promise is a trial for you, to see how you will act, or an enjoyment for you ﴿for a time﴾, so that it may be a proof against you, and so that the promise may occur at a time in which it is wise.

The passage is read as "qul" and "qāla," as a quotation of the words of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It is read as "Rabbi uḥkum" with only the kasra (short i-vowel) on the final consonant, as "Rabbu uḥkum" with a damma, and as "Rabbī aḥkam," in the elative form (ʾafʿal al-tafḍīl, the comparative/superlative pattern). "Rabbī aḥkam" is derived from al-iḥkām (judging, deciding).

It is an order to hasten the punishment for his people, and they were punished at Badr. The meaning of "bil-ḥaqq" is: do not show them favour, and be severe against them as they deserve. This is like what he said (ﷺ): "Make your trampling harsh upon Muḍar." [Agreed upon (by al-Bukhari and Muslim) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah concerning the story of the qunut in the dawn prayer.]

"Taṣifūna" is read with both the ta' and the ya'.

They used to describe the situation contrary to how it actually was. They hoped that power and victory would be theirs, so Allah belied their assumptions, frustrated their hopes, granted victory to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers, and humiliated them.

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites *iqtarab lil-nāsi ḥisābuhum* (the Qur'an's verse beginning "The reckoning of people has drawn near"), Allah will reckon with him with an easy reckoning, and every prophet whose name is mentioned in the Qur'an will shake his hand and greet him with peace." [Recorded by al-Thaʿlabi and Ibn Mardawayh from the hadith of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb.]
